item.title: Distro choice doesn’t matter anymore, and that’s why 2027 is the year Linux finally goes mainstream
item.itunes:title: Distro choice doesn’t matter anymore, and that’s why 2027 is the year Linux finally goes mainstream
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The first question that gets asked of a Windows user switching to Linux is which distro to install, and for many years, that was the correct one. It used to decide whether your Wi-Fi card would work or your games would launch first try, but now, it has lost a lot of its weight, and I think that's a good thing.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've run many Linux distros on my desktop over the years, and I've settled on CachyOS for a multitude of reasons, but most of those are niche and specific to me. For someone who sees Ubuntu or Fedora and thinks it looks comfortable and welcoming, the best experience they can have on those distros can almost certainly match mine, and the only difference nowadays is defaults, most of which can be easily changed. That shift, more than any single distro getting better, is what gives 2027 a real chance of being the year Linux goes mainstream.

5 awesome Linux features that will blow the mind of a Windows user

Don't know much about Linux? Get ready to blow your mind!

3
By  Rich Edmonds

The parts you actually use are pretty much the same everywhere

Linux has most of what you need regardless of distro

Most new users will interact with parts of a Linux system that don't belong to a single distro. Flathub is a great example of this, and it works as a shared app store across distros, so the same build of Firefox, OBS, or Discord installs and behaves the same way on Fedora, Mint, or an Arch derivative.

For gamers, Steam goes a step further by adding Proton, a compatibility layer that hands a Windows game a standardized set of libraries regardless of the distro running underneath. If I go to run something like Cyberpunk 2077 on a machine running Ubuntu and then one running vanilla Arch, so long as both have the proper GPU drivers, they should run and behave the same way.

The host distro mostly just supplies the kernel, those graphics drivers, and core services like audio. On AMD and Intel hardware, even GPU drivers are the same upstream kernel and Mesa code everywhere; distros differ mainly in how recent a version they ship. Add in the fact that many distros today support either KDE Plasma or GNOME, and what a newcomer might think of as "the OS" is largely a shared experience across dozens of distros.

There are still day-to-day distro differences I've run into, but they're becoming less common as the years go by. For the Ubuntu 26.04 mini PC I run, Snap is the primary format for packages. It's the default for installing software, and the App Center lists Snap and Deb packages but leaves Flatpak out until you add it yourself. On CachyOS, which is the OS on my main workstation, you're pointed toward pacman and the wider Arch ecosystem, but you can easily install AppImages, too.

Steam is a better way to run Windows apps on Linux than Wine, and it's not just for games

Proton is just better Wine

10
By  João Carrasqueira

A lot of users probably won't be picking a distro

Valve might be the reason for that

Perhaps the biggest shift we might see is that the choice of distro is made before the user enters the picture. Valve’s Steam Machine launched at the end of June 2026 running SteamOS, and anyone who buys one gets Linux without ever hearing or seeing the word "distribution."

SteamOS 3.8 extended that to self-built PCs with AMD graphics, which would help those who want to experience it outside their Steam hardware do so. The scale is still quite modest, and the level to which other OEMs sell machines with Linux as the installed OS is still dwarfed by their Windows sales, but it's trending upward.

5 reasons why 2025 might finally be the year of the Linux desktop

Despite their small share in the consumer PC landscape, 2025 is shaping up to be a solid year for Linux distributions

33
By  Ayush Pande

Why 2027, specifically

Windows 10 is on the way out, for real this time

Every year has been the year of the Linux desktop. It's obviously a bit of a running joke, but in late 2027, there may be an exodus from Windows 10 due to extended security support lapsing. Microsoft recently extended free consumer Extended Security Updates by another year, and coverage now ends on October 12, 2027. That makes late 2027 the real deadline for the large base of PCs that work perfectly well but can’t officially run Windows 11, and unless Microsoft drops the system requirements that bar these systems, it'll be one of the best natural on-ramps for Linux that we've seen in a while.

Microsoft quietly gave Windows 10 another year, but it can't keep kicking the can down the road

Old PCs gain another year of security updates as memory costs climb and the Windows 11 path stays narrow.

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

You still probably shouldn't dice-roll your distro

At least, not yet

Anti-cheat is the main barrier that gets brought up when it comes to Linux adoption by gamers, and it's not unwarranted, but there's growth on that front. Epic announced Easy Anti-Cheat Linux v2 in October 2026, with Fortnite as its first test. Epic hasn’t committed to a date, but if it lands in 2027, that'll only add to the optimism surrounding the platform.

However, with that said, it also happens to be a reason why you shouldn't just pick your distro blindly out of a hat. EAC Linux v2 requires Secure Boot and a kernel signed by an organization whose key Epic recognizes, and that list covers the big players like Canonical, Fedora, and Universal Blue distros. My desktop wouldn't be a candidate, as CachyOS ships its own tuned kernel, so I wouldn't be able to play, though the developers behind CachyOS are building one. The Steam Deck doesn’t meet the requirements yet either, though Epic says it’s talking with Valve to iron that out.

Then there's Nvidia, which I've conveniently ignored thus far. Getting full performance out of your GPU still means using the proprietary driver, and each distro handles this a bit differently. There are some distros which provide dedicated install images with Nvidia drivers included, and others will install them automatically.

3 reasons Linux is the best alternative to Windows for gamers

Linux is still the best option for gamers looking to get away from Microsofts grasp

6
By  Elliot Alexander

Choose based on support for the things you actually use

Distro choice mattering less than ever is a big part of why Linux could see real growth in 2027, and if you’re switching over from Windows yourself, it has never been easier. Pick a mainstream distro that has the desktop environment you're looking for, get your apps from its software store and your games from Steam, and stop thinking about it.

item.title: You can now build your own Linux desktop with HTML and CSS, and it looks better than KDE Plasma
item.itunes:title: You can now build your own Linux desktop with HTML and CSS, and it looks better than KDE Plasma
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Chromium is everywhere. I'm using it to edit and publish this very article. There's a good chance you're using a Chromium-powered browser to read it. Google exercises considerable control over web publishing technologies through this initiative, which may not sound like such a bad idea on paper, but it's also responsible for a high-revenue ad-publishing business. Ad-blockers beware! Still, Chromium is solid, and you can now design and put together your own Linux desktop using HTML and CSS.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Why, I hear you ask? Well, why not? I decided to take Domicile for a spin.

Making a Linux distro look like a website

Well, not really, but you get the idea...

Linux distributions (distros) come in all shapes and sizes. You've got the option of having a one-click installer that'll have you up and running in no time. There are also distros like Arch Linux that provide a blank canvas for you to configure your own Linux OS installation with various custom integrations. Want a tiling window manager? Give Hyprland a try. Fancy yourself a free and open-source OS that looks like Apple's macOS? That's also possible.

Then there are setups that try something truly unique and different, such as Domicile. It's not really a Linux distro of sorts, but more an experimental Linux desktop where a modified Chromium is the Wayland compositor. If that sounds ridiculous, it's because it is. Native apps, websites, and the desktop's own interface are elements on one web page, laid out with CSS and composited together. It's like ChromeOS, where everything is centralized around web tech.

Wayland windows as DOM elements. Chromium as the compositor. May God have mercy on our souls.

If you're at all familiar with web technology, such as CSS and HTML, you'll feel right at home with Domicile. Once you've chosen your favorite flavor of Linux (I went with the tried and tested standard of Debian), installing and running Domicile is incredibly easy. Simply add the repository, install Domicile, and launch the shell. I logged out and back in with Domicile running alone instead of on top of Wayland. The latter is how it'll be when you're messing with initial files, but it's much better to run a dedicated session.

Hyprland's biggest strength is also why I'm switching back to KDE

With great power comes great responsibility

4
By  João Carrasqueira

Running Chromium within Chromium

Look, Ma, no hands!

I really like tile-based desktop environments (DEs) like Sway and River. They're great at getting more done simultaneously without having to drag around windows and figure out where that one Google Chrome tab is located. Domicile is a little like that off the bat with its default configuration. It reminds me very much of ChromeOS (with Google's newer Googlebook OS now taking a different direction) with its emphasis on the web and the present tabbed layout. What's interesting is Firefox outright refused to let the mouse interact with the browser.

For whatever reason, Firefox wouldn't respond to mouse clicks in my installation. After a single command, I was now running Chromium on Domicile via Chromium. RAM is a little on the heavy side, as one would expect. 3GB as a baseline and about 3.5GB with a few smaller website tabs open within Chromium. But configuring everything is fairly painless. If you're used to working with CSS, it'll feel much more familiar than something like Hyprland. Npm is used to share packages too, everything from launchers to an entire desktop.

It's pretty neat and something new to try when looking at how best next to switching things up on your Linux machine. While not perfect (and developed with the assistance of AI), Domicile is already shaping up to be quite the entry point for making something run a little like ChromeOS, but without all the limitations that come with it. If you own a compatible Google Chromebook (x86-64), this could be something worth considering to maintain that free experience without losing too much from a traditional desktop.

Customizing Domicile with CSS is surprisingly easy

Who needs a conventional desktop theme anyway?

What makes Domicile particularly interesting is how much control you have over the desktop's appearance and behavior. Most Linux desktop environments allow you to customize the interface through themes, extensions, and configuration files. Domicile takes a different approach by treating the entire desktop as a web page. If you know your way around CSS, you can create some truly bizarre setups without having to learn how to write a traditional Wayland compositor.

The default Manganese shell provides an excellent starting point, but you can build your own shell using React, HTML, and CSS. For example, CSS Flexbox and Grid can be used to arrange application windows, while properties such as border-radius, box-shadow, and filter can adjust how those windows appear. One setup could be as simple as having a side-by-side two-app layout or as complex as recreating Windows Phone on desktop, designing your own minimalist tiling desktop, or making Linux look like a futuristic control panel.

7 tools to make your Linux desktop look amazing

Make your desktop uniquely yours.

5
By  Joe Rice-Jones

It's not replacing KDE Plasma just yet

I love KDE. It's customizable, looks smart as default, and doesn't tax the system too much. Domicile is experimental software, and my experiences with Firefox refusing to respond to mouse input demonstrate that there are still some rough edges to contend with. There's also the obvious question of resource consumption, given that we're essentially using Chromium to manage our entire desktop. Having said that, it's an interesting project that demonstrates just how flexible Linux can be.

Do I believe you should give it a go in a virtualized environment or even toy with a Chromebook that could run it? Absolutely.

item.title: I gave my old PC games path tracing with RTX Remix, and they look better than DLSS 5
item.itunes:title: I gave my old PC games path tracing with RTX Remix, and they look better than DLSS 5
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've spent the last few weeks forcing DLSS 5 into games that were never designed for it, so naturally, my next terrible idea was to go in the opposite direction. Instead of bringing Nvidia's latest neural rendering tricks to modern games, I decided to see what happens when you give some of my favorite old PC games a completely new lighting system.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I'd been meaning to try RTX Remix for almost two years, but I never got around to it until now. Thankfully, three classic games in my own Steam Library had dedicated RTX Remix mods ready to play, and I couldn't believe my eyes when I finally played them.

RTX Remix makes old games look new again

The most ridiculous remaster you can make yourself

RTX Remix is essentially Nvidia giving modders a way to tear apart the rendering pipeline of older DirectX games and rebuild it with modern lighting. Instead of simply increasing texture resolution, Remix can replace old materials with physically-based ones and introduce full path tracing, turning decades-old scenes into something that can look surprisingly contemporary.

This isn't a conventional remaster, though. Nobody at Valve went back and rebuilt Half-Life 2 from scratch, after all. These are community-driven projects using Remix to fundamentally change how light behaves inside games that were never designed to handle it. We know that older games relied on baked lighting, static shadows, and clever visual tricks to create depth. RTX Remix takes that entire pipeline and replaces it with dynamically calculated lighting.

This is also where my DLSS 5 obsession comes in. I've already spent enough time watching Nvidia's neural rendering transform modern games that I wanted to see whether path tracing could do something even more impressive to games old enough to drink. After firing up these RTX Remix projects, I think I may have found exactly that.

Path tracing is slowly becoming a non-negotiable for me, and it wouldn't be possible without DLSS

Never thought I'd say this, but if it's got path tracing, I want it on.

17
By  Samarveer Singh

Getting RTX Remix to work is only half the battle

The magic happens after the game has already rendered

RTX Remix works by intercepting the rendering calls made by compatible DirectX 8 and 9 games, and effectively replacing their ancient fixed-function rendering pipeline with a modern one. From there, Remix adds physically based materials, path-traced lighting, and Nvidia's upscaling and ray reconstruction technologies without requiring developers to rebuild the entire game.

For my testing, I used my RTX 4070 Ti system, which is still a surprisingly capable little torture chamber for this sort of experiment. Half-Life 2 RTX and Portal with RTX were straightforward enough to get running, since they have simple Steam pages for downloading the RTX Remix mods.

Depending on how much work a modder has put into a game, an RTX mod's assets, lighting, materials, and compatibility can vary wildly. Max Payne was particularly stubborn, because getting a community-made Remix project running isn't quite as simple as installing a Steam game and pressing Play.

Clearly, RTX Remix isn't magic. The framework provides the tools, but someone still has to rebuild the assets and make everything behave. When it works, though, the difference between the original renderer and a fully path-traced version can be ridiculous.

RTX Remix, when done right, trumps DLSS 5

Half-Life 2 RTX is still the star of the show

Half-Life 2 RTX is technically unfinished, with the current mod limited to Ravenholm and Nova Prospekt, but I genuinely don't think that matters. These two chapters are among the best demonstrations I've seen of what modern lighting can do for a 2004 game. Ravenholm in particular feels almost unrecognizable once every light source starts behaving like an actual light source.

Every flickering flame and creepily swinging lightbulb in the RTX Remix version of Ravenholm is breathtaking, and it's nothing short of a modern-day remake. The performance hit is, naturally, hilarious. My RTX 4070 Ti went from around 900 FPS to just 111 FPS with path tracing enabled. That's a ridiculous drop, but it's also par for the course, especially with anything with the "RTX" prefix in its name. The number that matters is 111 FPS, not the frankly useless 900 FPS I started with.

More importantly, even multiple DLSS 5 neural rendering passes couldn't replicate what Nvidia achieved here. Path tracing fundamentally changes how Ravenholm is lit, shaded, and ultimately perceived, and that's a much bigger transformation than another layer of neural rendering could provide.

For Portal RTX, the transformation is just as dramatic, although it hits differently. Portal's sterile test chambers were already built around clean surfaces, bright lights, and reflective materials, which makes them almost perfect for path tracing. The portals themselves are the obvious showstopper, but the way light spills through the chambers, bounces off surfaces, and interacts with the environment made me stop and stare.

As with Half-Life 2, the price of admission was performance. Portal RTX absolutely hammered my GPU, but the visual difference it offered in exchange for that path-tracing tax was worth it and then some. And after seeing what Remix does here, I was starting to understand why comparing it with DLSS 5 isn't nearly as straightforward as I initially thought.

I ran DLSS 5 on my PS2 games, and they finally looked like I remembered them

Nostalgia, meet neural rendering

11
By  Samarveer Singh

RTX Remix is more than a nostalgia trip

After spending time with RTX Remix, I don't think it's fair to call these projects simple visual upgrades anymore. It is a fundamentally better way of presenting environments that were already brilliantly designed. That doesn't mean everyone should start installing Remix mods, though.

You still need an RTX GPU with enough horsepower to absorb the considerable performance hit, and even then, community projects can involve enough troubleshooting to make a normal remaster look wonderfully convenient. I'd personally draw the line at an RTX 40-series card, especially if you want to run path tracing without turning your graphics settings into a negotiation.

item.title: I stuck a $10 USB LED strip to the back of my monitor, and my evening eye strain completely disappeared
item.itunes:title: I stuck a $10 USB LED strip to the back of my monitor, and my evening eye strain completely disappeared
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
An evening session in a dark room with a single high-brightness monitor can create extreme local contrast. Your pupils dilate to adjust to the dark room while taking in direct bright light from the display, which can cause digital eye strain and fatigue.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Common attempts to fix this problem include overhead lighting and desk lamps, which can introduce glare, panel reflections, and unequal spatial illumination that washes out the screen's contrast. I opted instead for an inexpensive USB-powered LED strip taped to the back of my panel, providing enough bias lighting to reduce eye strain during long evening workflows and gaming sessions.

You might be straining your eyes

Bias lighting could be the solution

Human visual perception calculates contrast dynamically based on the total area of the visual field, not just the single light source you're focusing on. This means that even though you're staring at a bright screen, your eyes are also adjusting for the dark room around you.

According to visual calibration and grading practices, such as light illusion recommendations, surrounding a display with ambient light equal to or roughly 10% of the display's maximum luminance may reduce pupil constriction fatigue. Having around 15 to 20 nits of back wall lighting behind a 150- to 200-nit screen is roughly in line with elevating the background illumination. As a result, you narrow the dynamic luminance step between the monitor and the surrounding environment, allowing your pupil to stay stable and relaxed.

It also increases the perceived contrast ratio. Human visual perception deepens black levels relative to surrounding light sources, so by adding bias lighting behind your screen, you can mask inherent backlight bleed and a low static contrast ratio. Dark tones, especially near the screen's edges, can visually collapse into deeper blacks due to the optical contrast illusion. This can reduce the impact of IPS glow without altering the monitor's physical hardware output.

Unlike front-facing or overhead lights, a rear-mounted LED strip bounces light off the wall behind the monitor, acting as a broad, indirect diffuse radiator that largely avoids the glare of front or overhead lighting.

I didn't know I needed a monitor light bar until I got one

I never thought it would make such a big difference

7
By  Sumukh Rao

What LED strip should you pick up?

Funnily enough, you don't need the best of the best

Picking up a budget-friendly USB LED strip is the easiest way to tackle this problem. I decided to pick up a standard 5 V DC-operated strip drawing power via a USB Type-A port. This let me plug it into a downstream monitor USB port and enabled synchronous power cycling. I don't have to worry about switching the light on and off independently.

It instead automatically cuts power to the LED strip when my display is switched off. If you want your display to do the same thing, make sure it cuts power to its USB ports when it's off or in standby, since not all do. Low overall power consumption also means minimal thermal dissipation to consider, and I don't have to worry about thermal degradation of the plastic chassis or any of the internal display driver electronics.

The industry reference standard for bias lighting is 6,500K, also known as the D65 white point. Most budget-friendly strips use fixed cool white LEDs, typically spec'd around 6,000K to 6,500K. However, ultra-cheap LED strips often use lower-quality phosphors that can drift toward 7,000K to 8,000K and, as a result, emit an uncalibrated blue spectral peak. This might lead to a color shift or a colder cast, so I'd personally avoid them.

My eyes thanked me for the change

And I didn't have to deal with glare

After installing this budget-friendly LED strip, I found that over several weeks of evening use, whether that was writing, terminal navigation, or just gaming, my eyes felt significantly less strained and irritated. Before installing the bias lighting, I struggled with a lot of eye strain, forced squinting, and dry eyes. Sometimes, particularly during long gaming sessions, I would get headaches too, likely as a result of these issues with my eyes.

I felt like I was no longer dealing with these issues, likely because I wasn't straining my eyes as much. While bias lighting doesn't directly address the dryness, I think the reduced strain definitely helped.

Although I don't have an OLED panel, my perceived black level improved immensely too. Dark scenes in games and films had far less noticeable backlight bleed, making for a much more pleasant experience. I often avoid turning on overhead lighting because of the glare, and it was nice not to have to worry about that anymore.

You don't need to invest in pricey lighting ecosystems

A simple LED strip made a major change to my setup

Fixing digital eye strain doesn't require expensive RGB ambient ecosystems like Philips Hue or Corsair ICUE smart lighting. These can easily cost over $100. A basic, budget-friendly 5V USB LED strip may address the fundamental physiological root cause of visual strain by elevating background ambient lighting, narrowing the spatial contrast ratio, and eliminating pupil-adaptation fatigue.

Its impact on my daily visual comfort, image contrast perception, and overall eye health has made it one of the highest-value, lowest-cost modifications I have made to my desktop workstation.

item.title: Mesh Wi-Fi is the worst way to start a home network if you can run even one cable
item.itunes:title: Mesh Wi-Fi is the worst way to start a home network if you can run even one cable
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Mesh Wi-Fi is touted as a shortcut for good home Wi-Fi without running cables everywhere, and in some ways, it can be. The hardware has earned a reputation for being pretty decent out of the box, but mesh nodes talk to each other over the same airwaves your phone, laptop, and TV are competing for, which could pose performance issues depending on deployment.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The solution isn't to avoid using mesh Wi-Fi, but to stop relying on it entirely over the air. If you can run even just one Ethernet cable, your network will serve you a lot better, and you might not need a mesh system at all, at least not one that's completely wireless.

Can you have too many mesh network nodes?

Mesh networks are a great way to enhance connectivity, but how many nodes is too many?

4
By  Ty Sherback

Wireless backhaul eats the airtime your devices are looking for

The airwaves are a shared medium

Wi-Fi is a shared medium where everything on one channel is competing for airtime, and radios can't transmit and receive on the same channel at the same moment. When a satellite node relays traffic back to the main router wirelessly in a mesh, every packet goes out twice, which uses up this valuable airtime that your devices would otherwise get.

On a dual-band mesh system where one radio handles both clients and the link back to the router, that relay can cut usable throughput roughly in half at each hop in the chain, so you can see how this can become problematic in a hurry. A second hop in a daisy-chained setup compounds the loss even more, and even though tri-band and quad-band kits soften this, it's still a wireless link, and its performance depends on distance, walls, and interference.

Each hop in the chain also adds obvious latency and jitter, but it also kills speed. Even if the speed test near a satellite looks fine, a game session or video call on that same node can be a complete nightmare.

I replaced my mesh Wi-Fi with a single high-end router, and the results surpassed my expectations

Performance improvements were well worth the switch.

12
By  Chandraveer Mathur

The real problem is your router's location

Most bad home Wi-Fi can be traced back to this

The truth is, the reason why your Wi-Fi sucks probably starts at the router level, and there's a good chance it's not because of the hardware itself, but where it's physically placed.

The internet line usually enters a home at a corner, in a basement, or in a utility room, and the router ends up beside it, sending much of its signal toward places nobody uses. Wireless mesh tries to fix placement by adding radios, but it brings a placement problem of its own. A satellite has to be close enough to the main node to keep a strong backhaul link, yet far enough away to extend coverage meaningfully. That's a bit of a catch-22, and many satellites end up halfway between the router and dead zone, which ensures neither job gets done well.

A single cable can remove this compromise almost completely. A wired access point’s connection to the router doesn’t depend at all on signal strength, so you can place it purely based on where you need coverage. All of its radio capacity goes to the surrounding clients, and the same cable run can also feed a small switch at the far end, giving a TV, console, or desktop a wired connection instead of adding yet another wireless client.

Mesh Wi-Fi is the most expensive way to fix a dead zone, and one wired access point beats it on almost everything

A mesh network can be a costly upgrade to fix a minor coverage issue

3
By  Tanveer Singh

Separate gear can also outlast a mesh system

You're not tied down to an ecosystem

A router and standalone AP are two independent purchases, and to me, make more sense than a mesh system when moving past starter gear. When a faster internet plan arrives, you can replace the router and keep the access point, and when a new Wi-Fi generation becomes worth having, you can swap the access point and keep the router.

Mesh kits also tend to tie you down to an ecosystem, meaning the nodes will generally only mesh with other hardware from that vendor. Additionally, control and management lives within their app, and they can even lock features like security filtering or parental control behind subscriptions.

Standalone access points from prosumer lines usually offer more control, such as multiple SSIDs and VLAN support for separating smart home gadgets from your main devices. Many can also be powered over the Ethernet cable through PoE, so the one cable carries both data and power, which can make the run even simpler.

5 reasons I’d always choose mesh Wi-Fi over a traditional router

When it comes to routers, I’d choose a mesh router every time. Here’s why.

12
By  Cierra Noffke

Mesh is still fantastic for some homes

Don't discount the right mesh system deployed the right way

For many, running a cable simply isn't an option, and that's where mesh has a real advantage. You might be a renter who can't drill or have a house where fishing cable is a big mission, and in these situations, a mesh system is an improvement over a single router. Mesh is also a bit simpler to get up and running. Setup happens in one app and the system moves devices between nodes on its own, with updates also taking place on their own without your input.

6 reasons you should replace your router's Wi-Fi with APs or mesh

If you've got a big house or specific Wi-FI needs, you might want to consider some upgrades.

4
By  Joe Rice-Jones

One cable can mean coax, not just Ethernet

You're not limited to running UTP

Credit: Source: MoCA Alliance

You might not be able to run Ethernet cable, but there's a good chance you already have coaxial cable somewhere. MoCA adapters turn existing coaxial TV wiring into an Ethernet-like link, and it works surprisingly well.

One adapter connects to the router and a nearby coax jack, the other connects to a jack in the target room, and the device at the far end sees an ordinary Ethernet connection. Current MoCA 2.5 hardware supports multi-gigabit speeds with low, consistent latency, which is much closer to a real cable than to a wireless hop. It also works as backhaul for a mesh node, as long as the system supports wired backhaul through its Ethernet port.

Powerline adapters also exist, though their effectiveness really depends on your house's electrical wiring. Real-world speeds are usually a fraction of the number on the box, and results depend heavily on the age of the wiring and whether both adapters share a circuit. Powerline can work well in one house and barely work in the next, so your mileage will vary.

Mesh Wi-Fi is causing the exact problems it promised to solve

Why does my home still have dead zones?

19
By  Jasmine Mannan

Start with a cable if you can, then decide on a mesh

For anyone moving past starter networking gear, going straight to a mesh isn't always the right option. It's a great way to get wireless networking coverage where cables aren't an option, but if they are, even in a limited capacity, it's worth considering that route first. A router and AP setup or even a semi-wired mesh can be much better than a completely wireless one.

item.title: Fake memory cards are everywhere, and here's how to spot them
item.itunes:title: Fake memory cards are everywhere, and here's how to spot them
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Your latest laptop may not have an SD card slot, but memory cards haven't gone anywhere. They celebrated their 25th anniversary last year, selling over 12 billion units in 25 years. Whether it's SD, microSD, or CFexpress cards, these ultra-compact flash storage cards power everything from phones and handhelds to SBCs, digital cameras, and drones.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Unfortunately, counterfeit memory cards are also more common than ever. It's not even that hard to make a fake memory card — some cheap flash storage and tampered firmware are all that's needed to fool most people. Your fake memory card may have only a fraction of the storage capacity and read/write speeds you paid for. To protect your data, it's essential to inspect your memory card before you deploy it for regular use.

Please stop buying the fastest SD card for your Raspberry Pi

It might seem worth it to grab the fastest SD card for your Raspberry Pi, but the benefits don't outweigh the cost.

12
By  Madeline Ricchiuto

Memory cards are still relevant in 2026

And so is the corresponding counterfeit industry

  • Credit: Source: Wikimedia Commons
  • Credit: Source: Wikimedia Commons

I remember using memory cards extensively during the 2010s, extending my smartphone storage to accommodate more data than my phone natively could. The first digital camera I bought, a Nikon point-and-shoot, used an SD card. Even my first laptop, which I got for my MBA, had an SD card slot. While smartphones moved on to faster and more robust memory, other consumer devices still depend on a variety of memory cards.

High-resolution digital cameras, action cameras, and drones use SDXC or microSDXC cards to meet modern storage and performance demands. Gaming handhelds, such as the Steam Deck, use microSDXC cards in addition to supporting SSDs. Then, there are SBCs like the Raspberry Pi, which typically see microSDHC and microSDXC cards for storage and booting.

With the continued proliferation of memory cards came the persistent waves of counterfeits. Scammers can not only spoof the firmware and design of memory cards but also the packaging to shockingly convincing results. Even if you buy from official channels, getting a fake is not impossible, since counterfeit cards can find their way to genuine stock, getting mixed and sold from the same channels.

6 signs the SSD you're about to buy is fake

Spot the signs before you spend your dough

2
By  Chandraveer Mathur

You can protect yourself from fakes using free tools

No need to spend even more money

The simplest test against fake memory cards is CrystalDiskMark. This tool can benchmark your memory card to reveal its true read/write speeds. If it's significantly lower than what the card is supposedly capable of, you know that something is wrong. CrystalDiskMark simply writes a small test file to a memory card's flash storage, so you can't use it to know the card's true capacity.

For that, you'll need to rely on ValiDrive. This free utility is a spot-check tool designed to quickly detect spoofed capacities on storage devices. It works by writing data to random sectors of the memory card, USB drive, or SSD, to detect mis-advertised capacity. It chooses sectors throughout the reported capacity, so it's all but guaranteed to spot, say, a 512GB card posing as a 64GB one.

Then, there's h2testw, which is a longer but more comprehensive tool to rule out the possibility of a fake memory card. It reads and writes across every single sector of the card for a thorough inspection, detecting a counterfeit card easily. It can take several hours to complete, depending on the card's capacity.

4 things you should do when you receive a new hard drive

From manufacturing defects to sellers listing used HDDs as new, buying a hard drive can devolve into a painful experience if you aren't careful enough

6
By  Ayush Pande

You don't always need to buy a fake to spot it

Being extra cautious is recommended

The tools I listed above only work when you've paid for the memory card and can test it on your machine. However, there are some precautions you can take even before parting with your money. For starters, ignore deals that list cards for way cheaper than comparable models. For instance, 512GB SD cards usually go for around $100, but you can spot some listings for less than $40 from unknown brands and third-party sellers. It's safe to skip those completely.

When shopping in offline stores, you can inspect the packaging before buying a memory card. Examine the pack for typos and wrong color tones. Fake cards will also have poorly printed serial numbers and other text on the package. While checking online for serial number authenticity doesn't tell you anything (scammers can copy genuine serials on millions of packages), the quality of the packaging can help you detect a counterfeit in most cases.

Counterfeit GPUs are on the rise: Here's how they work and how to tell if you have one

Counterfeit GPUs are becoming more common, and here's how they work and how to tell if you have one.

By  Adam Conway

Counterfeit memory cards aren't going anywhere, so you need to get smarter

The global counterfeit industry is valued at around $467 billion, and electronics are a frequent target. Counterfeit memory cards will continue to populate online and offline stores, so you need to stay vigilant. By avoiding shady listings, testing a card as soon as you get it (so you can return it if possible), and buying only from reputable channels will allow you the best chance to stay a step ahead of the scammers.

The SanDisk 1TB microSDXC card gives you up to 1TB of additional storage capacity on any device with a microSDXC card reader.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Corsair has brought its fantastic build quality to the fighting game scene, and the result is the Novablade Pro, a feature-heavy fightpad that targets the pros but welcomes anyone chasing frame-perfect combos. Right now, Amazon has knocked the price down to $190, which saves you $60 off the regular $250 list price. That's a solid discount for a premium controller with Hall Effect switches and tri-mode wireless connectivity.

Wireless?
Yes
Battery
Up to 40 hours (RGB on), up to 200 hours (RGB off)
Connectivity
USB-C wired, 2.4GHz wireless, Bluetooth
Programmable Buttons
15 main keys, 8 programmable G-keys

The Corsair Novablade Pro Wireless is a leverless fight controller that uses MGX Hyperdrive Hall Effect magnetic switches rated for 150 million presses. It has 15 buttons and 8 programmable G-keys, actuation adjustable from 0.1mm to 4.0mm, and 1000Hz polling when wired.

See at Amazon

What's so great about the Corsair Novablade Pro?

Easy to use, easy to customize

Credit: CORSAIR

The leverless layout on the Novablade Pro isn't just a gimmick. By removing the analog joystick entirely, Corsair reduces wrist strain and enables quicker complex moves than a traditional stick offers. The 15-button layout covers all your bases without clutter, and the anodized aluminum top plate keeps it planted during heavy combos. It weighs in at 1.4 kg, so it has a premium heft that stays put on your lap.

In addition to the leverless design, the Corsair Novablade Pro features Hall Effect magnetic switches. You get per-key actuation adjustment from 0.1mm to 4.0mm, plus rapid trigger that resets keys after just 0.1mm of upward travel. In fighting games, that translates to faster double-taps and cleaner inputs. The FlashTap SOCD tech handles opposing directional inputs, which is a lifesaver when you're mixing up pressure strings.

Emulating arcade games is harder than emulating consoles, and MAME's 30-year history shows why

Emulating a Super Nintendo is easy, but emulating an arcade cabinet is a different beast

3
By  Samarveer Singh

The Novablade Pro's RGB features look great and also indicate your settings, such as the actuation point, so you can check your configuration at a glance. PC players get the full treatment with macro recording and deeper customization, though you'll need to visit Corsair's site for updates since there's no iCUE software support.

At $190, the Novablade Pro may seem like a steep entry for a niche peripheral, but if you're serious about competitive fighting games and want tournament-grade precision without the bulk of a traditional stick, this deal price is more than worth it. Grab it while the price holds.

item.title: I turned Obsidian into an AI browser, and it does what Gemini in Chrome does without my research leaving my vault
item.itunes:title: I turned Obsidian into an AI browser, and it does what Gemini in Chrome does without my research leaving my vault
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Gemini has been living in Chrome's side panel since Google's big update back in January, and it's since rolled out to most of the world outside Europe. You can have it open beside whatever tab you have open and ask about the page without having to copy anything back and forth to a chatbot app. Google has been adding Personal Intelligence on top of that, which lets Chrome remember context from past conversations and tailor its answers to you.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The catch with browser assistants like this is that the page you're reading gets sent off to someone else's servers every time you ask about it, and with memory switched on, a running picture of your research ends up there too. This is where a local LLM comes in for private work, and with a web MCP you're already halfway there. However, Obsidian is where all my notes and docs are, plus, it already has a full browser built-in. This workflow is a little DIY because it's not an AI browser as much as it is AI bolted onto a browser feature - but it works seamlessly.

I replaced Google search with a local LLM for a week, and it changed how I find answers

The web, minus the scrolling and ads

By  Nolen Jonker

Obsidian already has a browser built-in

One of the most underrated Obsidian core plugins

Obsidian has a built-in browser as a core plugin, called Web Viewer, and it's been there since Obsidian 1.8 came out in early 2025. I've known about it, but overlooked it for most of the time I've been an Obsidian user. I already have Chrome for work and Brave for personal use, and constantly test AI browsers, so this one just disappeared into the background for me, until recently. It's built on Electron, which already bundles Chromium, so Web Viewer is basically a Chromium webview (the same feature Canvas uses to embed web pages) loaded into a regular Obsidian tab.

Once you've turned it on, you can easily access it from a fresh page or the command palette. A page can sit in a split beside the note you're writing, which I think is the biggest appeal of this feature. But you can also just use it like you would a regular browser, or perhaps pop it out into its own window if you have a second monitor. The glasses icon switches to a reader view that strips the page to plain text with Mozilla's Readability library (the same one behind Firefox's reader mode), and a save option turns the page into a note in your vault. Ad blocking is on by default too which is always appreciated.

I recommend checking the Open external Links setting to what you prefer. It decides whether links in your notes open inside Obsidian or get sent to your normal browser. And you can set your search engine preference while you're at it.

I turned Obsidian into my personal operating system with just one vault

One vault to organize absolutely everything.

2
By  Parth Shah

Copilot is the part that actually reads the page

Local model or cloud API, the plugin doesn't really mind which

Web viewer on its own just shows pages, so the AI has to come from somewhere, and that's going to be the Copilot plugin. It's a community plugin by Logan Yang (no relation to Microsoft's Copilot), which can attach whatever page is open in Web viewer to a chat the same way it attaches a note.

It's a BYOK situation, so to add a model you just go to its settings, pick LM Studio or Ollama from the list, which will fill in the local server address for you, and add your model name. For local options, there's no API key needed, which is the route I went with, but cloud providers work too if you'd rather paste in an API key. And my models of choice here are Qwythos 9B and Qwen 3.5 9B, which are pretty much my staples for bringing into local tools. I've got them set to 30k context in LM Studio, which strikes a good balance on my 8GB card.

The chat view you want is Quick Chat, which you open from the command palette and dock next to your Web Viewer tab. In its free Chat mode, whatever page you have open gets attached automatically, so there's nothing to copy over. It only answers from what's attached, though, so it won't search your vault unless you add a note yourself.

I de-Googled my life for a week, and this is the local setup that replaced search, photos, and documents

Taking a break from the company that controls half of my digital existence

By  Nolen Jonker

What a vault-aware browser can actually do

The page is only half of the context

Day to day, it comes down to a page in one tab and the Copilot panel docked beside it. The page is basically just like any other note that I'd bring my local LLM into. Its entire text goes in with the prompt and also gets sent again when a new page loads, so I can browse around a site and keep asking questions without having to re-attach anything. Be mindful that this can quickly drain your context budget, so what I like to do is hit the little New Chat button at the bottom when the topic changes.

The part Gemini can't match is what else goes into that chat. Typing @ pulls in other notes, whole folders, or other open web tabs, so a page can sit right next to my own notes on the same topic. For example, I can open a UX article and ask what it covers that my notes don't, or whether it contradicts something I wrote months ago. This goes beyond just getting basic summaries or explainers because now the answer partly depends on what's also in my vault. Two web tabs in the same chat turn it into a comparison tool for pricing pages or competing docs, and selecting a paragraph attaches only that bit, which helps with stuff like READMEs which sometimes go over my head.

Copilot lets you save prompts you trigger with a slash, and a saved prompt can pull in a specific note. If you keep a specific note, a command can audit whatever page is open against it, so a live site gets judged by your own criteria. Those chats autosave as Markdown notes too, which is how they end up back in the vault.

There are limits to this though. Copilot only reads the pages, it can't act on them. So you're not getting Gemini's auto browse here, where it clicks through sites on your behalf (that's a paid Google AI Pro and Ultra feature anyway). Long pages are the other thing. A small local model can only hold so much in context, and even when it can handle it, speed also becomes a factor - Qwythos 9B often took its sweet time to reply on moderate-length web pages.

My local LLM didn't replace my $20 Claude subscription, it replaced everything I was never comfortable sending to the cloud

There are many things Qwen3.6 struggles with, but keeping my data safe isn't one of them

10
By  Abhinav Raj

My research tabs found a new home

I still use Gemini in Chrome because that's the browser where a lot of my real work lives. But a lot of my research tabs have drifted to Obsidian now, which wasn't even entirely the plan when I switched Web Viewer on. I think the reason is pretty boring. A chat that lands as a note next to the notes it was about is a pretty cool function to have in my vault, plus the whole pipeline is private so long as I keep the AI layer local.

Free normally; $4/month for Obsidian Sync

You can have it open beside whatever tab you have open and ask about the page without having to copy anything back and forth to a chatbot app. Google has been adding Personal Intelligence on top of that, which lets Chrome remember context from past conversations and tailor its answers to you.

The catch with browser assistants like this is that the page you're reading gets sent off to someone else's servers every time you ask about it, and with memory switched on, a running picture of your research ends up there too. This is where a local LLM comes in for private work, and with a web MCP you're already halfway there. However, Obsidian is where all my notes and docs are, plus, it already has a full browser built-in. Obsidian already has a browser built-in

item.title: I connected my 3D printer to Home Assistant and Spoolman, and my self-hosted apps now track every gram of filament I use
item.itunes:title: I connected my 3D printer to Home Assistant and Spoolman, and my self-hosted apps now track every gram of filament I use
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Home Assistant may be a killer smart home management platform, but once you load it with the right set of integrations and apps, it can even accommodate non-IoT paraphernalia. On the self-hosted front, it can pair with everything from Jellyfin, Nextcloud, and llama.cpp to entire home lab platforms like Proxmox and TrueNAS. But if you’re as much of a 3D printing enthusiast as I am, you’ll find a bunch of cool first- and third-party integrations for your model-making companion.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

In fact, I’ve got my Elegoo Centauri Carbon 1 and 2 hooked up to HASS, and it makes managing their prints quite easy with its neat dashboards and trigger-action automations. But since I also use a self-hosted Spoolman container to maintain an inventory of all the filament spools in my 3D printing arsenal, I figured I could use its Home Assistant integration to track filament usage on my smart home platform. If that sounds intriguing, then here’s my log of configuring all the integrations and automations needed for this filament tracking pipeline.

5 things I 3D printed for my home lab that fixed problems I'd been living with

A 3D printer was a surprisingly useful investment for my home lab

3
By  Ayush Pande

Filament tracking on Home Assistant required a couple of integrations

The Elegoo and Spoolman integrations work well right off the bat

Seeing as how we’ve got multiple services relying on Home Assistant, this setup needs a bunch of integrations to run. For the 3D printers, I needed to get the elegoo-homeassistant integration by developer danielcherubini up and running, and with HASS moving the Home Assistant Community Store (and its offerings) to the built-in Marketplace, configuring this integration is even simpler now.

For my CC1, I simply tossed the 3D printer’s IP address into the integration configuration page, and Home Assistant was able to track its filament sensors, webcam, and other aspects on a custom dashboard. However, I had to enable LAN-only mode on my Centauri Carbon 2 and use its IP address and access code to pair the 3D printer with the integration, as the cloud mode would cause issues due to the fact that it uses Elegoo’s server for authentication.

Spoolman also needs a third-party integration in the form of spoolman-homeassistant by developer Disane87. Installing it is just as simple as the Elegoo integration, and I was able to see my spools as soon as I added my Spoolman’s IP address to Home Assistant.

By now, I was done setting up my integration arsenal, and if I were to rely on the OpenCentauri firmware on my CC1, I’d be able to configure the filament tracker automation chains without any issues. However, the Centauri Carbon 2 is what I rely on the most for my DIY shenanigans, and this printer needed another tool before I could start messing around with templates and automation rules.

I also had to deploy a printer proxy server for my CC2

So far, my game plan was to send filament consumption details from my Centauri Carbon 2 to Spoolman. But the biggest issue with such a setup is that my CC2 could only report total filament used statistics, which can mess up my Spoolman records every time I switch to a different feeding tube on its AMS-like CANVAS system. Since the elegoo-homeassistant can’t check the filament consumption metrics for each CANVAS tube on its own, I had to bring the elegoo-printer-proxy package by lantern-eight into the equation.

This containerized tool captures the G-code details, including the filament consumption stats and sends them to Home Assistant (and by extension Spoolman), thereby helping HASS get an estimation of the amount of filament my 3D printing siphons when turning STL files into tangible models.

Deploying this proxy server was fairly simple, too. First, I ran the git clone https://github.com/lantern-eight/elegoo-printer-proxy command to pull the package on a local VM. Then, I opened the compose.yml file using the nano editor and changed the subnets on all the IP address fields to match the one used by my home network.

For the printers, I opened the .env.cc1 and .env.cc2 files and changed the IP address fields to match the network details of my Centauri Carbon 1 and 2, respectively. I also had to assign the IP addresses of the proxy servers to my VM's Ethernet adapter, so I executed sudo ip addr add IP_address dev ens18. Then I ran sudo docker compose up -d --build to finally deploy the proxy server.

If you’re wondering why my security-conscious self had to resort to a rootful Docker setup, it’s because the rootless mode results in networking errors when Docker sets up access to all the proxy server ports under 1024. But since I’m using an isolated virtual machine just to host the proxy server, I don’t need to worry too much about the security implications of running Docker with full admin privileges. Finally, I added the proxy server’s URL to the elegoo-homeassistant integration before using it to replace the CC2’s IP address in my Elegoo Slicer.

But the automations themselves were fairly easy to configure

I had to keep the filament names consistent though

With the proxy server and integrations in tip-top shape, it was time to turn my attention to the trigger-action rules I’d need for this setup. Since the elegoo-homeassistant integration has detailed documentation on filament tracking, I had no issues replicating the templates and automation workflows on my setup.

First, I pasted the rest_command and helper template into the configuration.yaml file of my Home Assistant hub using the File Editor app. I also added the per-slot Spoolman weight template for each feeding tube before reloading my HASS setup.

Then, I configured the Update Spoolman From Filament Name script, which is responsible for deducting the filament used from my Spoolman hub. As for the automations, I added the YAML code for Cache CC2 Slot Data to Home Assistant before editing the IDs of the sensor.centauri_carbon_2_a1_grams and other filament tracker entities to match the names on my setup.

I also entered the code for the Reset CC2 Slot Cache automation to clear the cache after each print, while the CC2 Spoolman Update automation calls the Update Spoolman From Filament Name script every time a print is complete.

However, it took me a few failed attempts to realize that the trigger-action pipeline only works when the filament name on Spoolman matches the one on my Elegoo Slicer. So, after ensuring my naming scheme remains consistent throughout the automation workflow, I quickly created a benchy model to test the pipeline. And sure enough, Home Assistant was able to notify Spoolman about the filament utilization metrics after successful prints.

The setup process was definitely worth the extra effort

Considering that my Home Assistant + Spoolman combo not only tracks my filament stats in real time, but it even displays my spool inventory in custom dashboards, I’m satisfied with this automation pipeline. It may seem a bit convoluted on paper, but the overall process is fairly simple if you’ve ever tinkered with Docker containers and HASS integrations.
